case.title: Silver Blaze
case.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
case.summary: Silver Blaze, favourite for the Wessex Cup, has vanished from the King's Pyland stables on Dartmoor, and his trainer John Straker has been found dead on the moor with his skull crushed, a knife in one hand and a stranger's cravat in the other. The stable-lad on guard was drugged with opium in his supper. The police have arrested Fitzroy Simpson, a bookmaker who was seen at the stables that evening trying to bribe his way to a tip. Holmes is asked to find the horse and the murderer.
case.solution_summary: Straker, deep in debt from a secret second household kept under the name William Derbyshire, planned to lame his own horse so it would lose the race he had bet against. He chose curried mutton for supper so the opium he put in the stable-lad's portion would not be tasted, went down to the stables at night (the dog knew him, so it did not bark), and led Silver Blaze to a hollow on the moor to nick a tendon with a cataract knife by the light of a candle. When he struck a match behind the horse, Silver Blaze lashed out and killed him; his own knife cut his thigh as he fell. The horse bolted towards Mapleton, where its rival's trainer Silas Brown found it at dawn, hid it and disguised it. Simpson's cravat had been dropped as he fled and picked up by Straker. Holmes forces Brown to run the disguised horse, which wins.

time_model.day_zero: The Monday of the crime. The horse vanished in the early hours of day 1 (Tuesday).

days.label: The supper, the tout at the window, the drugging
source: Such was the general situation last Monday night when the catastrophe occurred.

days.label: Straker goes out at 1 a.m. and dies; the stable found open at 7; Simpson arrested; Holmes telegraphed in the evening
source: On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross

days.label: Holmes waits in London for the horse to be found, and wires about the stable door
source: I sent a special wire to Dartmoor yesterday to clear the matter up

days.label: Holmes and Watson travel down, investigate, and return by the night train
source: And this is Thursday morning.

days.label: The race at Winchester ("four days later"; see inconsistencies)
source: Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train, bound for Winchester to see the race for the Wessex Cup.

entities.name: Sherlock Holmes
entities.description: Consulting detective; invited by Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory.

entities.name: Dr. Watson
entities.description: Narrator. A doctor: identifies the cataract knife.

entities.name: John Straker
entities.description: Trainer at King's Pyland; retired jockey; five years Ross's jockey, seven his trainer.
entities.secret: Keeps a second household as 'William Derbyshire' with an extravagant woman, is deep in debt, and plans to lame Silver Blaze.
source: The trainer, John Straker, is a retired jockey

entities.name: Mrs. Straker
entities.description: Straker's wife. Saw him leave at 1 a.m.

entities.name: Edith Baxter
entities.description: The Strakers' maid. Carried the curried mutton to the stable; met the stranger.
source: the maid, Edith Baxter, carried down to the stables his supper

entities.name: Ned Hunter
entities.description: The stable-lad on guard that night; drugged.
source: the third, Ned Hunter, remained on guard

entities.name: The two other stable-lads
entities.description: Slept in the loft over the harness-room; heard nothing.

entities.name: A King's Pyland stable-lad
entities.description: Attends to the sheep in the paddock; tells Holmes three are lame. (The text does not say which lad.)

entities.name: Colonel Ross
entities.description: Owner of Silver Blaze. Sceptical of Holmes.

entities.name: Inspector Gregory
entities.description: "Extremely competent" but lacking imagination. Holds the police theory.

entities.name: Fitzroy Simpson
entities.description: Gentleman bookmaker who squandered a fortune on the turf; the 'tout' at the window; arrested.

entities.name: Silas Brown
entities.description: Trainer at Mapleton, of Desborough. A 'bully, coward, and sneak'.
entities.secret: Found Silver Blaze at dawn and hid him at Mapleton.

entities.name: Dawson
entities.description: A Mapleton groom.

entities.name: Madame Lesurier
entities.description: Bond Street milliner; identifies Straker's photograph as her customer 'Derbyshire'.

entities.name: "Mrs. Derbyshire"
entities.description: The 'very dashing wife' of Straker's second household. Never appears.

entities.name: Lord Backwater
entities.description: Owns Mapleton and Desborough.

entities.name: A party of gypsies
entities.description: Camped within a mile of the hollow on Monday night; gone on Tuesday.

entities.name: Silver Blaze
entities.description: Five-year-old of the Isonomy stock; favourite for the Wessex Cup; white forehead and mottled off-foreleg.

entities.name: Bayard
entities.description: King's Pyland's other Cup entry; scratched before the race.

entities.name: Desborough
entities.description: Mapleton's horse; second favourite.

entities.name: The stable dog
entities.description: Kept in the King's Pyland stable. Set on the tout; silent when Straker came at night.

entities.name: Sheep in the paddock
entities.description: Three have recently gone lame -- Straker's practice subjects.

entities.name: Railway carriage (Paddington-Exeter; later a Pullman car home)
Tavistock
entities.description: Two miles west of King's Pyland.

entities.name: King's Pyland training stables
entities.description: Colonel Ross's small establishment: four horses, three lads.

entities.name: Straker's villa
entities.description: About two hundred yards from the stables.

entities.name: The knoll near the house
entities.description: From it all the neighbouring moors are visible.

entities.name: The hollow where Straker died
entities.description: Bowl-shaped depression a quarter of a mile from the stables; furze-bush on its brink.

entities.name: The long hollow towards Mapleton
entities.description: Wet on Monday night; holds the horse's tracks.

entities.name: Mapleton training stables
entities.description: Lord Backwater's larger establishment, two miles across the moor; managed by Silas Brown.

entities.name: The cluster of invalids' villas
entities.description: Half a mile north; Simpson was lodging there.

entities.name: The gypsy camp
entities.description: Within a mile of the hollow.

entities.name: Dish of curried mutton
entities.description: Ned Hunter's supper; the household had the same.

entities.name: Simpson's folded white paper
entities.description: Offered for the boy. Simpson says it was a ten-pound note.

entities.name: Red and black silk cravat
entities.description: Simpson's; found in Straker's left hand.

entities.name: Simpson's stick
entities.description: A Penang-lawyer weighted with lead.

entities.name: Cataract knife
entities.description: Ivory-handled, delicate inflexible blade, marked Weiss & Co., London; tip guarded by a cork disk.

entities.name: Silver Blaze's bridle
entities.description: Missing.

entities.name: A duplicate stable key
entities.description: Posited by the police theory; never found.

entities.name: A cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze
Spirits of wine
entities.description: Washes the disguise off the horse.

entities.name: Milliner's account
entities.description: £37 15s, Madame Lesurier of Bond Street, made out to William Derbyshire; includes a 22-guinea costume.

entities.name: Contents of Straker's pockets
entities.description: Vestas, candle, briar pipe, seal-skin pouch, silver watch, five sovereigns, aluminium pencil-case, papers (three hay-dealers' accounts, a letter from Ross, the milliner's bill), the cataract knife.

scenes.title: Breakfast at Baker Street
scenes.summary: Holmes announces he must go to Dartmoor; Watson joins him.
source: I am afraid, Watson, that I shall have to go

scenes.title: The train to Exeter: the facts of the case
scenes.summary: Holmes states the facts from the papers and telegrams, and the police theory. Watson suggests the knife wound was self-inflicted.
source: We are going well

scenes.title: Tavistock and the drive with Gregory
scenes.summary: Gregory gives the latest: Simpson's answers, the gypsies, Mapleton searched. Holmes falls silent and arrives 'day-dreaming'.
source: It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock

scenes.title: Straker's villa: the pockets and Mrs. Straker
scenes.summary: Holmes examines what Straker had in his pockets, including a cataract knife and a milliner's bill to 'William Derbyshire'. He tests Mrs. Straker about a dress.
source: Excuse me,

scenes.title: The hollow
scenes.summary: The overcoat was placed, not blown. Holmes finds a buried wax vesta, compares boots, pockets the horseshoe, and tells Ross to keep the horse entered.
source: A short walk across the moor took us to the hollow

scenes.title: Across the moor to Mapleton

when.text: the sun was beginning to sink

scenes.summary: Holmes reasons the horse must be at Mapleton, finds its tracks, then a man's tracks beside them looping towards King's Pyland and back. He confronts Silas Brown, who capitulates.
source: It's this way, Watson

scenes.title: The walk back
scenes.summary: Holmes tells Watson how he broke Brown: square-toed boots, Brown always first up, the horse recognised by its white forehead. He announces their return to London.
source: A more perfect compound of the bully, coward, and sneak

scenes.title: Departure: the photograph, the sheep, the dog
scenes.summary: Holmes asks for Straker's photograph, puts a question to the maid, asks about the sheep, and points Gregory to the dog in the night-time.
source: Not a word more could I draw from him

scenes.title: The Wessex Cup
scenes.summary: A horse in Ross's colours with no white hair wins. Holmes reveals it is Silver Blaze in disguise -- and that the horse is Straker's killer.
source: Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train

scenes.title: The explanation on the train home
scenes.summary: Holmes explains the curry, the dog, the knife, the bill, the sheep, the milliner, and the death in the hollow.
source: We had the corner of a Pullman car to ourselves that evening

when.text: five years as jockey and seven as trainer

events.summary: Straker serves Colonel Ross, first as jockey, then as trainer, with an apparently honest record.
source: He has served the Colonel for five years as jockey and for seven as trainer

events.summary: Straker sets up a second household as 'William Derbyshire' with a woman of expensive tastes and falls deeply into debt.
source: I at once concluded that Straker was leading a double life, and keeping a second establishment.
plunged him over head and ears in debt

events.summary: Straker plans to make money by laming his own favourite so that it loses (implicitly by betting against it through agents).
source: led him into this miserable plot

events.summary: Straker practises the tendon-nick on the sheep in the paddock; three go lame.
source: but three of them have gone lame, sir

events.summary: Simpson squanders a fortune on the turf and becomes a quiet bookmaker in London clubs.
source: who had squandered a fortune upon the turf

events.summary: Simpson has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer.
source: He has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer.

events.summary: Simpson lays bets of £5,000 against the favourite.
source: bets to the amount of five thousand pounds had been registered by him against the favourite

events.summary: Silas Brown places large bets on the race; he is no friend of Straker.
source: Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event

events.summary: Simpson comes to Dartmoor for information on the King's Pyland horses and Desborough, lodging at the villas.
source: he had come down to Dartmoor in the hope of getting some information about the King's Pyland horses

events.summary: A party of gypsies camps within a mile of the hollow.
source: a party of gypsies encamped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where the murder took place

events.summary: Curried mutton is served for supper in the Straker household that night -- chosen by Straker (or his wife), as only they could.
source: the only two people who could have chosen curried mutton for supper that night

events.summary: The horses are exercised and watered and the stables locked up.
source: the stables were locked up at nine o'clock

events.summary: Two lads go up to the trainer's house to sup in the kitchen; Ned Hunter stays on guard.
source: Two of the lads walked up to the trainer's house, where they had supper in the kitchen

when.text: after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy

events.summary: Straker puts powdered opium into the portion set aside for Hunter.
source: The opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy

events.summary: Edith Baxter carries the curried mutton across the moor to the stable, with a lantern. No drink: the lad on duty drinks only from the stable tap.
source: At a few minutes after nine the maid, Edith Baxter, carried down to the stables his supper

events.summary: Thirty yards from the stable, Simpson stops Edith, asks where he is, and offers her a dress if the boy gets a folded paper.
source: See that the boy has this to-night, and you shall have the prettiest frock that money can buy.

events.summary: At the stable window Simpson asks Hunter for a tip on Silver Blaze and Bayard.
source: Let me have the straight tip and you won't be a loser.

events.summary: Hunter goes to unloose the dog, locks the door behind him, and runs out with the hound; the stranger has gone. Edith, fleeing, sees the stranger leaning through the window.
source: He sprang up and rushed across the stable to unloose the dog.
The boy locked the door before he left it.

events.summary: Simpson, fleeing, drops his cravat.
source: Simpson in his flight had dropped his cravat

events.summary: Hunter eats the curried mutton and sinks into a drugged stupor.
source: Hunter was obviously under the influence of some powerful drug

events.summary: When the other lads return, Hunter sends word to Straker, who is excited and vaguely uneasy.
source: Straker was excited at hearing the account

events.summary: Heavy rain, no wind.
source: None; but very heavy rain.

events.summary: Straker dresses, tells his wife he is anxious about the horses, picks up the cataract knife from the dressing-table, and goes out in his mackintosh.
source: Mrs. Straker, waking at one in the morning, found that he was dressing
he had picked it up as he left the room

when.text: in the dead of the night

events.summary: Straker enters the stable -- the dog knows him and stays quiet, the lads sleep, Hunter is drugged -- bridles Silver Blaze and leads him out, leaving the door open.
source: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze

events.summary: Straker picks up Simpson's dropped cravat, perhaps to tie the horse's leg.
source: Straker had picked it up--with some idea, perhaps, that he might use it in securing the horse's leg

events.summary: In the hollow, where his light cannot be seen, Straker takes off his overcoat and lays it over the furze-bush.
source: Straker had led out the horse to a hollow where his light would be invisible.
He had already, in spite of the rain, taken off his overcoat

events.summary: Behind the horse, Straker strikes a wax vesta (to light his candle).
source: he had got behind the horse and had struck a light

events.summary: Frightened by the flare, Silver Blaze lashes out; the steel shoe strikes Straker on the forehead. Falling, Straker gashes his own thigh with the knife.
source: the steel shoe had struck Straker full on the forehead
as he fell, his knife gashed his thigh

events.summary: Silver Blaze bolts alone across the moor towards Mapleton, leaving tracks in the wet hollow.
source: Ah, it bolted, and was cared for by one of your neighbours.

when.text: according to his custom he was the first down

events.summary: Silas Brown, first up, sees a strange horse near Mapleton, recognises the white forehead, and starts leading it back towards King's Pyland.
source: he perceived a strange horse wandering over the moor
his first impulse had been to lead him back to King's Pyland

events.summary: Tempted, Brown turns back, hides the horse at Mapleton until after the race, and disguises it (the white forehead and mottled leg are covered).
source: how he had led it back and concealed it at Mapleton

events.summary: Mrs. Straker and the maid find the stable door open, Hunter in a stupor, the stall empty.
source: Mrs. Straker awoke at seven in the morning

events.summary: From the knoll the searchers see the coat on the furze-bush and find Straker's body in the hollow.
source: John Straker's overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush

events.summary: The gypsies are gone.
source: On Tuesday they were gone.

events.summary: Gregory arrests Simpson at the villas.
source: he promptly found and arrested the man upon whom suspicion naturally rested

events.summary: Colonel Ross and Inspector Gregory telegraph Holmes.
source: On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross

events.summary: Gregory searches every stable and outhouse within ten miles, Mapleton included, and finds nothing.
source: I have also examined every stable and out-house in Tavistock, and for a radius of ten miles.

events.summary: Holmes stays in London expecting the horse to be found -- his admitted blunder.
source: I could not believe it possible that the most remarkable horse in England could long remain concealed

events.summary: Holmes and Watson investigate on Dartmoor (see actions).
Broken by Holmes, Brown agrees to keep the horse safe and produce it for the race as instructed.
source: Your instructions will be done.

events.summary: The inquest on Straker is due (its outcome is never told).
source: The inquest is to-morrow.

events.summary: Holmes shows Straker's photograph to the milliner, who knows him as 'Derbyshire'.
source: When I returned to London I called upon the milliner

events.summary: The odds on Silver Blaze shorten from fifteen to one to three to one: 'somebody knows something'.
source: You could have got fifteen to one yesterday

events.summary: Ross scratches his other horse and stakes everything on Holmes's word.
source: We scratched our other one, and put all hopes on your word

events.summary: A bay with no white hair, in Ross's colours, wins the Wessex Cup by six lengths from Desborough.
source: passed the post a good six lengths before its rival

events.summary: Holmes reveals the winner is Silver Blaze in disguise, and names the horse as Straker's killer.
source: The real murderer is standing immediately behind you.

nodes.label: The stranger on the path
nodes.statement: A gentlemanly stranger in grey tweed, cloth cap and gaiters, with a heavy knobbed stick, very pale and nervous, stopped Edith thirty yards from the stable and offered her a dress if the boy got a folded white paper that night.
source: She was most impressed, however, by the extreme pallor of his face
See that the boy has this to-night

nodes.label: The tout at the window
nodes.statement: At the stable window the stranger asked Hunter for a tip about Silver Blaze and Bayard; Hunter called him a tout and went for the dog; Edith saw him leaning through the window; when Hunter ran out he was gone.
source: So, you're one of those damned touts!
saw that the stranger was leaning through the window

nodes.label: The paper in his hand
nodes.statement: Edith swears she saw the corner of the little paper packet in the stranger's closed hand as he spoke at the window.
source: the corner of the little paper packet protruding from his closed hand

nodes.label: A dog in the stable
nodes.statement: A dog is kept in the stable: Hunter went to unloose it against the stranger and ran out with the hound.
source: He sprang up and rushed across the stable to unloose the dog.
nodes.notes: Given in passing as part of the tout incident; its importance only appears with ev.lads_heard_nothing.

nodes.label: The door was locked
nodes.statement: Hunter locked the stable door behind him when he ran out with the dog, and the window is too small for a man to get through: the stranger could not have got in.
source: The boy locked the door before he left it.
The window, I may add, was not large enough for a man to get through.

nodes.label: The lads heard nothing
nodes.statement: The two lads asleep in the loft above the harness-room heard nothing during the night.
source: They had heard nothing during the night, for they are both sound sleepers.

nodes.label: Curried mutton
nodes.statement: Hunter's supper was a dish of curried mutton, carried down by Edith; no drink, since the lad on duty drank only from the stable tap.
source: which consisted of a dish of curried mutton
She took no liquid, as there was a water-tap in the stables

nodes.label: Opium in the leftovers
nodes.statement: Analysis of the remains of Hunter's supper shows an appreciable quantity of powdered opium; the people at the house ate the same dish that night without ill effect.
source: the remains of his supper left by the stable-lad contain an appreciable quantity of powdered opium
while the people at the house partook of the same dish on the same night without any ill effect

nodes.label: Hunter blames the stranger
nodes.statement: Hunter is certain the stranger drugged his curried mutton while standing at the window.
source: He was equally certain that the same stranger had, while standing at the window, drugged his curried mutton

nodes.label: Straker was uneasy
nodes.statement: Told of the tout, Straker was excited and vaguely uneasy.
source: Straker was excited at hearing the account

nodes.label: Out at one in the morning
nodes.statement: Mrs. Straker woke at one in the morning to find her husband dressing; he said he was anxious about the horses and would walk down to the stables, and went out into the rain in his mackintosh.
source: Mrs. Straker, waking at one in the morning, found that he was dressing
he pulled on his large mackintosh and left the house

nodes.label: Door open, stall empty
nodes.statement: At seven the stable door was open, Hunter was in a stupor on a chair, and the favourite's stall was empty.
source: The door was open; inside, huddled together upon a chair, Hunter was sunk in a state of absolute stupor

nodes.label: No bridle
nodes.statement: The horse's bridle is missing: whoever took him out bridled him.
source: His bridle is missing, so that Simpson must have put this on.

nodes.label: The horse has vanished
nodes.statement: Since Tuesday morning there is no news of Silver Blaze, despite a large reward and every gypsy on the alert; he is not back at King's Pyland.
source: But from that morning he has disappeared, and although a large reward has been offered

nodes.label: Coat on the furze-bush
nodes.statement: Straker's overcoat was found on a furze-bush at the brink of the hollow, a quarter of a mile from the stables -- laid across the bush.
source: John Straker's overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush
Yes, it was laid across the bush.

nodes.label: The body
nodes.statement: Straker's head was shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon, and he had a long, clean cut on the thigh from a very sharp instrument.
source: His head had been shattered by a savage blow from some heavy weapon
he was wounded on the thigh, where there was a long, clean cut

nodes.label: Bloody knife in his right hand
nodes.statement: In his right hand Straker held a small knife clotted with blood up to the handle.
source: in his right hand he held a small knife, which was clotted with blood up to the handle

nodes.label: Cravat in his left hand
nodes.statement: In his left hand Straker clasped a red and black silk cravat.
source: in his left he clasped a red and black silk cravat

nodes.label: The stranger's cravat
nodes.statement: Edith and, when he recovered, Hunter both identify the cravat as the one the stranger wore that evening.
source: which was recognised by the maid as having been worn on the preceding evening by the stranger
was also quite positive as to the ownership of the cravat

nodes.label: Hoofprints in the hollow
nodes.statement: Marks in the mud at the bottom of the hollow prove the horse was there at the time of the struggle.
source: there were abundant proofs in the mud which lay at the bottom of the fatal hollow that he had been there at the time of the struggle

nodes.label: £5,000 against the favourite
nodes.statement: Simpson's betting-book records bets of five thousand pounds against Silver Blaze.
source: bets to the amount of five thousand pounds had been registered by him against the favourite

nodes.label: Simpson's statement
nodes.statement: Simpson admits the scene at the stable but says he only wanted first-hand information on the King's Pyland horses and on Desborough, with no sinister design.
source: had simply wished to obtain first-hand information

nodes.label: Simpson turns pale
nodes.statement: Confronted with his cravat, Simpson turned very pale and could not account for its being in the dead man's hand.
source: When confronted with his cravat, he turned very pale

nodes.label: Simpson's wet clothes
nodes.statement: Simpson's clothing was wet: he had been out in the storm that night.
source: His wet clothing showed that he had been out in the storm of the night before

nodes.label: A loaded stick
nodes.statement: Simpson's stick is a Penang-lawyer weighted with lead -- just such a weapon as could have inflicted Straker's head wounds.
source: his stick, which was a Penang-lawyer weighted with lead

nodes.label: No wound on Simpson
nodes.statement: Simpson has no wound, though Straker's bloody knife suggests he marked one of his assailants.
source: there was no wound upon his person

nodes.label: A ten-pound note
nodes.statement: Simpson says the paper he wanted given to the boy was a ten-pound note; one was found in his purse.
source: He says that it was a ten-pound note. One was found in his purse.

nodes.label: Not a stranger here
nodes.statement: Simpson has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer, so he knows the district.
source: He has twice lodged at Tavistock in the summer.

nodes.label: "I lost it"
nodes.statement: Simpson acknowledges the cravat is his and says he had lost it.
source: He acknowledges that it is his, and declares that he had lost it.

nodes.label: No key found
nodes.statement: No duplicate stable key has been found on Simpson (Gregory supposes it was thrown away).
source: Has a duplicate key been found in his possession?
The key, having served its purpose, would be hurled away.

nodes.label: Gypsy camp traces
nodes.statement: Traces show a party of gypsies camped within a mile of the hollow on Monday night; by Tuesday they were gone.
source: a party of gypsies encamped on Monday night within a mile of the spot where the murder took place

nodes.label: Brown's bets
nodes.statement: Silas Brown of Mapleton, trainer of the second favourite, has large bets on the race and was no friend of Straker.
source: Silas Brown, the trainer, is known to have had large bets upon the event, and he was no friend to poor Straker

nodes.label: Mapleton searched: nothing
nodes.statement: Gregory has searched every stable within ten miles, Mapleton included, and found nothing connecting Brown to the affair.
source: We have, however, examined the stables, and there is nothing to connect him with the affair.

nodes.label: Simpson and Mapleton unconnected
nodes.statement: Nothing connects Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables.
source: And nothing to connect this man Simpson with the interests of the Mapleton stables?

nodes.label: Straker's pockets
nodes.statement: Straker's pockets held a box of vestas, two inches of tallow candle, a briar pipe, a pouch of tobacco, a silver watch, five sovereigns, a pencil-case, some papers, and an ivory-handled knife.
source: There was a box of vestas, two inches of tallow candle

nodes.label: A cataract knife
nodes.statement: The knife from Straker's hand is a cataract knife (Weiss & Co.): a very delicate, inflexible blade that would not shut in a pocket; its tip had been guarded by a cork disk found beside the body.
source: It is what we call a cataract knife
The tip was guarded by a disk of cork which we found beside his body

nodes.label: Taken from the dressing-table
nodes.statement: Mrs. Straker says the knife had lain on the dressing-table and Straker picked it up as he left the room.
source: His wife tells us that the knife had lain upon the dressing-table, and that he had picked it up as he left the room.

nodes.label: A bill for 'William Derbyshire'
nodes.statement: Among Straker's papers is a milliner's account for £37 15s from Madame Lesurier of Bond Street, made out to William Derbyshire -- including twenty-two guineas for a single costume.
source: a milliner's account for thirty-seven pounds fifteen made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire
Twenty-two guineas is rather heavy for a single costume.

nodes.label: "A friend of my husband's"
nodes.statement: Mrs. Straker says Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's whose letters were sometimes addressed to the house.
source: Derbyshire was a friend of her husband's and that occasionally his letters were addressed here
nodes.notes: What Straker told her. It is a cover story.

nodes.label: "I never had such a dress"
nodes.statement: Asked (by a pretended memory of a garden-party) about a dove-coloured silk costume with ostrich-feather trimming, Mrs. Straker says she never had such a dress.
source: You wore a costume of dove-coloured silk with ostrich-feather trimming.
I never had such a dress, sir

nodes.label: No wind that night
nodes.statement: There was no wind that night, only very heavy rain.
source: There was no wind that night, I understand
None; but very heavy rain.

nodes.label: A burnt match in the mud
nodes.statement: Buried in the trampled mud of the hollow is a half-burned wax vesta, so coated it looks like a chip of wood. Holmes found it because he was looking for it.
source: It was a wax vesta half burned
I only saw it because I was looking for it.

nodes.label: Boot impressions
nodes.statement: Holmes compares Straker's boot and Simpson's shoe with the marks in the hollow. (The result is not stated.)
source: compared the impressions of each of them with marks upon the ground

nodes.label: Hoofprint towards Mapleton
nodes.statement: In the soft earth of the long hollow towards Mapleton is a horse's track, which Silver Blaze's cast shoe fits exactly.
source: the shoe which he took from his pocket exactly fitted the impression

nodes.label: A man's track joins it
nodes.statement: Close to Mapleton a man's track appears beside the horse's (which was alone before). The double track turns off towards King's Pyland, then comes back the opposite way and ends at the asphalt before the Mapleton gates.
source: A man's track was visible beside the horse's.
The double track turned sharp off and took the direction of King's Pyland.
It ended at the paving of asphalt which led up to the gates of the Mapleton stables.

nodes.label: Square toes
nodes.statement: The man's prints have peculiarly square toes, and Silas Brown's own boots correspond exactly.
source: the peculiarly square toes in the impressions, and that his own boots exactly corresponded to them
nodes.notes: Holmes says 'of course you observed' -- the reader is told only afterwards.

nodes.label: Always the first stirring
nodes.statement: Brown's groom says that if anyone at Mapleton is about at five in the morning, Brown will be: he is always the first stirring.
source: if any one is about he will be, for he is always the first stirring

nodes.label: Brown breaks
nodes.statement: Brown starts violently, flushes, calls Holmes's whispered words 'an infernal lie', then after twenty minutes inside comes out ashen and trembling, promising 'It shall be there' and asking whether to change 'it' first.
source: He started violently and flushed to the temples.
Should I change it first or not?

nodes.label: Three lame sheep
nodes.statement: The lad who tends the sheep in the paddock says three of them have recently gone lame.
source: but three of them have gone lame, sir

nodes.label: The odds shorten
nodes.statement: On race day the odds on Silver Blaze have shortened from fifteen to one to about three to one, then five to four.
source: You could have got fifteen to one yesterday

nodes.label: Not a white hair
nodes.statement: The horse running in Ross's colours has not a white hair on its body -- yet Silver Blaze is known by his white forehead and mottled off-foreleg.
source: A child would know Silver Blaze, with his white forehead and his mottled off-foreleg.
That beast has not a white hair upon its body.

nodes.label: The milliner knows him
nodes.statement: Madame Lesurier recognises Straker's photograph as her excellent customer 'Derbyshire', who had a very dashing wife with a taste for expensive dresses.
source: the milliner, who had recognised Straker as an excellent customer of the name of Derbyshire, who had a very dashing wife

nodes.label: Watchdogs bark at strangers
nodes.statement: A stable dog is kept to raise the alarm against intruders; it barks at strangers but not at people it knows well.
source: I'll show you how we serve them in King's Pyland.
nodes.notes: Never stated outright; implied by Hunter setting the dog on the tout.

nodes.label: Opium can be tasted
nodes.statement: Powdered opium is not tasteless: mixed into an ordinary dish it would be noticed and the eater would stop.
source: Powdered opium is by no means tasteless.
Were it mixed with any ordinary dish the eater would undoubtedly detect it, and would probably eat no more.

nodes.label: Curry hides the taste
nodes.statement: A curry is exactly the medium that would disguise the taste of opium.
source: A curry was exactly the medium which would disguise this taste.

nodes.label: Without wind, a coat does not blow
nodes.statement: A coat cannot be blown onto a bush on a windless night; if it is on the bush, someone put it there.
source: In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.

nodes.label: What a cataract knife is for
nodes.statement: A cataract knife is a surgical instrument for the most delicate operations; no sane man would choose it as a weapon.
source: A very delicate blade devised for very delicate work.
used for the most delicate operations known in surgery

nodes.label: Nicking a tendon
nodes.statement: A slight subcutaneous nick to the tendons of a horse's ham leaves no trace and causes a lameness that is put down to strain or rheumatism, never to foul play.
source: it is possible to make a slight nick upon the tendons of a horse's ham
but never to foul play

nodes.label: Trainers who bet against their horses
nodes.statement: Trainers have made great sums by laying against their own horses through agents and then stopping them from winning by fraud.
source: trainers have made sure of great sums of money by laying against their own horses, through agents

nodes.label: A pricked horse is loud
nodes.statement: So spirited a horse, pricked with a knife, would rouse the soundest sleepers; the operation had to be done in the open air.
source: would have certainly roused the soundest of sleepers when it felt the prick of the knife

nodes.label: Nobody carries another man's bills
nodes.statement: Men do not carry other people's bills in their pockets; they have enough to do settling their own.
source: men do not carry other people's bills about in their pockets

nodes.label: A trainer's wage
nodes.statement: A trainer in service cannot afford twenty-guinea walking dresses for his lady.
source: one can hardly expect that they can buy twenty-guinea walking dresses for their ladies

nodes.label: Practise first
nodes.statement: A careful man would not attempt so delicate an operation without first practising.
source: would not undertake this delicate tendon-nicking without a little practice

nodes.label: Horses go home
nodes.statement: A horse is a gregarious creature: left to itself it would go back to its own stable or to the nearest other stable, not run wild on the moor.
source: The horse is a very gregarious creature.
If left to himself his instincts would have been either to return to King's Pyland or go over to Mapleton.

nodes.label: Gypsies avoid trouble
nodes.statement: Gypsies clear out at the first sign of trouble to avoid the police, and could never sell so famous a horse: taking him would be all risk and no gain.
source: These people always clear out when they hear of trouble
They could not hope to sell such a horse.
nodes.notes: Period prejudice, stated by Holmes as a general rule. Flag for any adaptation.

nodes.label: Wet ground keeps tracks
nodes.statement: Hard dry turf keeps no tracks; a hollow that was wet on Monday night will.
source: there is a long hollow over yonder, which must have been very wet on Monday night

nodes.label: Faker's dye
nodes.statement: A horse-faker can hide a horse's markings with dye that spirits of wine will wash off.
source: You have only to wash his face and his leg in spirits of wine
Oh, an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge.

nodes.label: Telegraph posts
nodes.statement: The telegraph posts on this line are sixty yards apart.
source: the telegraph posts upon this line are sixty yards apart

nodes.label: 53½ miles an hour
nodes.statement: The train is going fifty-three and a half miles an hour.
source: Our rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour.
nodes.notes: Holmes's method on display; no bearing on the case.

nodes.label: The coat was placed
nodes.statement: The overcoat was not blown onto the bush; Straker took it off and laid it there himself.
source: In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.

nodes.label: The drugger knew about the curry
nodes.statement: Whoever drugged Hunter must have known curry would be served that night, because only curry hides the taste of opium.
source: it is surely too monstrous a coincidence to suppose that he happened to come along with powdered opium upon the very night when a dish happened to be served which would disguise the flavour

nodes.label: Simpson did not drug the lad
nodes.statement: Simpson, an outsider, could not have caused curry to be served in the trainer's household, so he did not drug the lad.
source: Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case

nodes.label: Drugged after it was dished up
nodes.statement: The opium was added after Hunter's portion was set aside, since the household ate the same dish without effect.
source: The opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy

nodes.label: The drugger was Straker or his wife
nodes.statement: Only Straker and his wife could have chosen curried mutton for supper that night; the drugger is one of them.
source: our attention centres upon Straker and his wife, the only two people who could have chosen curried mutton for supper that night

nodes.label: The dog knew the visitor
nodes.statement: Someone came in at night and took out a horse, yet the dog did not bark enough to wake the lads in the loft: the midnight visitor was someone the dog knew well.
source: To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.
Obviously the midnight visitor was some one whom the dog knew well.
nodes.notes: Pointed at in s08 ('the curious incident'), explained in s10.

nodes.label: Straker took out the horse
nodes.statement: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of night and took out Silver Blaze.
source: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze

nodes.label: Straker drugged his own lad
nodes.statement: Of the two in the household, it was Straker who drugged Hunter -- he is the one who then went to the stable and took the horse.
source: or why should he drug his own stable-boy?

nodes.label: His purpose was dishonest
nodes.statement: Straker took the horse out for a dishonest purpose -- an honest trainer does not drug his own stable-boy.
source: For a dishonest one, obviously, or why should he drug his own stable-boy?

nodes.label: The knife was for an operation
nodes.statement: Straker deliberately took a cataract knife, useless as a weapon, because he meant to perform a delicate operation that night.
source: And it was to be used for a delicate operation that night.

nodes.label: He meant to lame the horse
nodes.statement: Straker meant to nick Silver Blaze's tendon so the horse would go lame and lose, with no trace of foul play.
source: it is possible to make a slight nick upon the tendons of a horse's ham

nodes.label: Out on the moor, by candlelight
nodes.statement: The operation had to be done in the open, away from the sleeping lads, in a hollow where a light would not be seen -- hence the candle and the vestas.
source: It was absolutely necessary to do it in the open air.
Of course that was why he needed the candle, and struck the match.

nodes.label: Is Derbyshire Straker?
nodes.statement: 'William Derbyshire' is Straker himself, keeping a second establishment with an extravagant woman.
source: I at once concluded that Straker was leading a double life, and keeping a second establishment.

nodes.label: Straker WAS Derbyshire
nodes.statement: Confirmed: Straker led a double life as William Derbyshire; the expensive dresses went to his second household, not his wife.
source: felt that by calling there with Straker's photograph I could easily dispose of the mythical Derbyshire

nodes.label: The motive: debt
nodes.statement: The extravagant second household had plunged Straker into debt, and that led him into the plot against his own horse.
source: I have no doubt that this woman had plunged him over head and ears in debt, and so led him into this miserable plot.

nodes.label: Did he practise on something?
nodes.statement: Straker practised the tendon-nick beforehand -- perhaps on the sheep.
source: What could he practice on? My eyes fell upon the sheep

nodes.label: He practised on the sheep
nodes.statement: Straker practised on the sheep in the paddock: three of them have gone lame.
source: showed that my surmise was correct

nodes.label: Straker picked up the cravat
nodes.statement: Simpson dropped his cravat as he fled; Straker picked it up, perhaps to secure the horse's leg. It does not place Simpson at the hollow.
source: Simpson in his flight had dropped his cravat, and Straker had picked it up

nodes.label: The horse killed him
nodes.statement: When Straker struck a light behind him, Silver Blaze lashed out and the steel shoe struck him on the forehead; falling, he gashed his own thigh with the knife. The horse killed him in self-defence.
source: The real murderer is standing immediately behind you.
the steel shoe had struck Straker full on the forehead

nodes.label: Simpson is innocent
nodes.statement: Simpson neither drugged the lad nor killed Straker; he was only a tout.
source: Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case

nodes.label: Not the gypsies
nodes.statement: The gypsies did not take the horse.
source: They would run a great risk and gain nothing by taking him.

nodes.label: Working hypothesis: Mapleton
nodes.statement: The horse bolted, and since it is not at King's Pyland it went to Mapleton.
source: He is not at King's Pyland. Therefore he is at Mapleton.
Let us take that as a working hypothesis

nodes.label: The horse went to Mapleton, alone
nodes.statement: Silver Blaze crossed the wet hollow alone, heading for Mapleton -- the prediction is confirmed.
source: We imagined what might have happened, acted upon the supposition, and find ourselves justified.

nodes.label: Someone met the horse
nodes.statement: Near Mapleton a man met the horse, began leading it towards King's Pyland, changed his mind, and took it into Mapleton.
source: saw to my surprise the same tracks coming back again in the opposite direction

nodes.label: The man was Silas Brown
nodes.statement: The man was Silas Brown himself: square-toed boots like his, always first up, and no subordinate would dare.
source: Again, of course no subordinate would have dared to do such a thing.

nodes.label: Brown is hiding Silver Blaze
nodes.statement: Silas Brown found the favourite at dawn, recognised it by the white forehead, and hid it at Mapleton to stop the only horse that could beat his.
source: chance had put in his power the only horse which could beat the one upon which he had put his money

nodes.label: The horse is disguised
nodes.statement: Brown hid the horse from Gregory's search by disguising its white markings; the winner with no white hair is Silver Blaze.
source: I found him in the hands of a faker, and took the liberty of running him just as he was sent over.

nodes.label: The police theory
nodes.statement: Simpson drugged the lad, opened the stable with a duplicate key, bridled the horse and led it off to kidnap it; met by Straker, he beat out his brains with his loaded stick, then hid the horse or let it bolt.
source: The police imagine, I take it, that this Fitzroy Simpson, having drugged the lad

nodes.label: Watson: a self-inflicted cut
nodes.statement: The cut on Straker's thigh was made by his own knife in the convulsions after the head injury.
source: that the incised wound upon Straker may have been caused by his own knife in the convulsive struggles
nodes.notes: Right that the knife was his own; wrong about the convulsions -- he cut himself as he fell. Holmes and Gregory both think it tells AGAINST Simpson's innocence.

nodes.label: Gregory: the gypsies have him
nodes.statement: Simpson was leading the horse to the gypsies, by arrangement, when Straker overtook him; the gypsies now have the horse.
source: might he not have been leading the horse to them when he was overtaken

nodes.label: Holmes's blunder
nodes.statement: So famous a horse cannot stay hidden on the moor: it will be found within hours, and its abductor will be the murderer.
source: From hour to hour yesterday I expected to hear that he had been found, and that his abductor was the murderer of John Straker.
the calculation is a simple one
In that case the overcoat was not blown against the furze-bush, but placed there.
That is unthinkable.

premises.note: Simpson is a stranger who meets the dish only on the path, already cooked.

source: By no possible supposition could this stranger, Fitzroy Simpson, have caused curry to be served in the trainer's family that night
for the others had the same for supper with no ill effects
Which of them, then, had access to that dish without the maid seeing them?
he had not barked enough to arouse the two lads in the loft

premises.note: The stranger could not have got in at the window.

source: I was already convinced, or almost convinced, that John Straker went down to the stables
or why should he drug his own stable-boy?
For a dishonest one, obviously
a knife which certainly no sane man would choose for a weapon
A horse so treated would develop a slight lameness
We have here the explanation of why John Straker wished to take the horse out on to the moor.
The nature of the bill showed that there was a lady in the case, and one who had expensive tastes.
having satisfied myself that it had never reached her
I have no doubt that this woman had plunged him over head and ears in debt
My final shot was, I confess a very long one.
I asked a question which, rather to my surprise, showed that my surmise was correct
with some idea, perhaps, that he might use it in securing the horse's leg
but the creature frightened at the sudden glare
Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case
And why should gypsies kidnap him?
He is not at King's Pyland. Therefore he is at Mapleton.
See the value of imagination
The horse was alone before
Again, of course no subordinate would have dared to do such a thing.
When I told him every detail he gave it up and thought only of saving his own skin.
Oh, an old horse-faker like him has many a dodge.
That is the case as it appears to the police
presuming that there was some understanding between Simpson and these gypsies
It is more than possible; it is probable,
Because I made a blunder, my dear Watson

relations.note: Suggests the drug was in the paper.
Answers Holmes's 'stranger to the district' objection.
Removes the 'no wound on Simpson' objection.
source: In that case one of the main points in favour of the accused disappears.

relations.note: Weakened if the knife cut was self-inflicted.
He could not have drugged anything from inside, nor slipped in.
'Somebody knows something' -- presumably Brown or his people backing the disguised horse.
Watson's guess was half right: the knife was Straker's own.

actions.summary: Mrs. Straker and the maid go down to the stables when Straker has not come back.
source: She dressed herself hastily, called the maid, and set off for the stables.

actions.summary: The lads and the two women search; from the knoll they see the coat and find the body in the hollow.
source: on ascending the knoll near the house, from which all the neighbouring moors were visible

actions.summary: The police take statements from the maid, Hunter (once recovered), the lads and Mrs. Straker.
The remains of Hunter's supper are analysed.
source: Finally, an analysis has shown

actions.summary: Gregory finds and arrests Simpson at the villas, examines his betting-book, stick and clothes, and takes his statement.
source: he promptly found and arrested the man upon whom suspicion naturally rested

actions.summary: Gregory finds the gypsy camp, scours the moor, searches every stable within ten miles (Mapleton included), and learns Simpson's history and Brown's bets.
source: The moor is being scoured for these gypsies.

actions.summary: Ross and Gregory telegraph Holmes asking for his help.
source: On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross

actions.summary: Holmes reads every edition of the papers and the telegrams, sifting fact from surmise -- and waits for the horse to turn up.
source: Fresh editions of every paper had been sent up by our news agent

actions.summary: Struck by the question of whether Hunter left the door unlocked when he ran out, Holmes sends a special wire to Dartmoor.
source: I sent a special wire to Dartmoor yesterday to clear the matter up

actions.summary: Holmes times the telegraph posts and gives the train's speed.
source: Our rate at present is fifty-three and a half miles an hour.

actions.summary: Watson suggests the thigh wound came from Straker's own knife.
source: that the incised wound upon Straker may have been caused by his own knife

actions.summary: Holmes and Watson take the train to Tavistock, where Ross and Gregory meet them.
source: It was evening before we reached the little town of Tavistock

actions.summary: In the landau Holmes puts his objections to the police case; Gregory answers them and adds the gypsies and Mapleton.
source: Has a duplicate key been found in his possession?

actions.summary: Arriving at the trainer's house, Holmes sits on in the carriage, 'day-dreaming': the significance of the curried mutton has struck him.

when.text: just as we reached the trainer's house

source: It was while I was in the carriage, just as we reached the trainer's house, that the immense significance of the curried mutton occurred to me.

actions.summary: Holmes grasps the silence of the dog, and from it that Straker himself took out the horse, for a dishonest purpose.
source: Before deciding that question I had grasped the significance of the silence of the dog

actions.summary: Holmes asks to see what Straker had in his pockets; Watson identifies the cataract knife; Gregory relays Mrs. Straker's statements about the knife and Derbyshire.
source: I presume that you made an inventory of what he had in his pockets at the time of his death, Inspector?

actions.summary: A cataract knife means a delicate operation; the operation is laming the horse; it must be done in the open by candlelight.
source: And they did so.

actions.summary: A man does not carry another man's bills: Straker is leading a double life.
source: I at once concluded that Straker was leading a double life

actions.summary: Holmes pretends to remember Mrs. Straker from a Plymouth garden-party in a dove-coloured silk costume; she has never had such a dress.
source: Surely I met you in Plymouth at a garden-party some little time ago, Mrs. Straker?

actions.summary: At the hollow Holmes asks about the wind: there was none, so the coat was placed on the bush.
source: There was no wind that night, I understand

actions.summary: Gregory hands over his bag: Straker's boot, Simpson's shoe, and a cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze.
source: In this bag I have one of the boots which Straker wore

actions.summary: Lying on the matting, Holmes searches the trampled mud -- looking for a match -- and finds a half-burned wax vesta.
source: he made a careful study of the trampled mud in front of him

actions.summary: Holmes compares the boots with the marks in the hollow and crawls about the rim.
source: He took the boots from the bag

actions.summary: Holmes tells Ross not to withdraw Silver Blaze from the Cup.
source: I should let the name stand.

actions.summary: Walking over the moor: the horse is gregarious, the gypsies would not take it, it is not at King's Pyland -- so, as a working hypothesis, it is at Mapleton.

when.text: The sun was beginning to sink

source: We may leave the question of who killed John Straker for the instant

actions.summary: Holmes and Watson search both banks of the wet hollow towards Mapleton; Holmes finds a hoofprint the horseshoe fits.
source: At Holmes' request I walked down the bank to the right, and he to the left

actions.summary: They follow the track; a man's prints join it; it turns towards King's Pyland -- Watson spots it coming back -- and ends at the Mapleton gates.
source: One for you, Watson

actions.summary: Holmes asks the groom Dawson whether Brown would be up at five tomorrow morning.
source: Should I be too early to see your master, Mr. Silas Brown, if I were to call at five o'clock to-morrow morning?

actions.summary: Holmes whispers to Brown what he did that morning, follows him inside for twenty minutes, and leaves him promising to keep the horse safe and produce it as instructed.

when.text: the reds had all faded into greys

source: Holmes leaned forward and whispered something in the trainer's ear.

actions.summary: With the vesta found and the horse accounted for, Holmes has the whole night's story: the cravat, the light, the kick. (He keeps it to himself.)
Holmes asks Gregory for a photograph of Straker.
source: Might I ask for a photograph of Mr. John Straker?

actions.summary: Holmes leaves the room to put a question to the maid. Neither question nor answer is ever told.

yields.unknown: The text never says what Holmes asked or learned.

source: I have a question which I should like to put to the maid

actions.summary: Straker would have practised first -- on what? Holmes's eyes fall on the sheep.
source: What could he practice on?

actions.summary: Getting into the carriage, Holmes asks the stable-lad whether anything is amiss with the sheep: three have gone lame.
source: Have you noticed anything amiss with them of late?

actions.summary: Holmes directs Gregory to the sheep and to 'the curious incident of the dog in the night-time'.
source: To the curious incident of the dog in the night-time.

actions.summary: Holmes and Watson return to London by the night train.
source: we both go back to London by the night train

actions.summary: In London Holmes shows Straker's photograph to the milliner on Bond Street.
source: When I returned to London I called upon the milliner

actions.summary: Holmes writes to Brown with his instructions (keep the disguise on; send the horse to the race).
source: I shall write to you about it

actions.summary: At Winchester the disguised horse runs in Ross's colours and wins; Holmes tells Ross to wash its face and leg in spirits of wine, and names the horse as Straker's killer.
source: Here he is,

actions.summary: On the train home Holmes explains everything to Ross and Watson.

questions.answer: John Straker, his own employer, after the dish was set aside.

questions.text: Who took Silver Blaze out of the stable?

false_answers.answer: Fitzroy Simpson, with a duplicate key

questions.text: Why was the horse taken out?
questions.answer: To lame it with a nick to the tendon, out on the moor where the noise and light would not be noticed, so that it would lose.

false_answers.answer: To kidnap it for the gypsies or a betting coup

questions.answer: Silver Blaze, in self-defence: kicked when Straker struck a light behind him.

false_answers.answer: Fitzroy Simpson, with his loaded stick

questions.answer: At Mapleton, hidden and disguised by Silas Brown.

false_answers.answer: Dead at the bottom of an old mine-pit

questions.answer: He was deep in debt from a secret second household as 'William Derbyshire'.
No. He was only a tout trying to buy a tip; he dropped his cravat as he ran.

inconsistencies.summary: The race is 'next Tuesday', but the narration puts it 'four days later' than the Thursday of the investigation -- a Monday.
inconsistencies.resolution_used: day 7 (Monday), following the narration; the Tuesday reading would be day 8.
source: preventing Silver Blaze from being there at the fall of the flag next Tuesday
I have every hope, however, that your horse will start upon Tuesday
Four days later Holmes and I were again in the train

inconsistencies.summary: The race is called the Wessex Cup throughout, but the race card names it the Wessex Plate.
source: the race for the Wessex Cup
Wessex Plate.

inconsistencies.summary: Holmes says Brown's horse 'bolted, and was cared for by one of your neighbours' while in s07 he says Brown deliberately hid it -- the first is Holmes softening it for Ross, under the 'amnesty' he grants.
source: Ah, it bolted, and was cared for by one of your neighbours.
We must have an amnesty in that direction

notes: Holmes keeps almost all his reasoning back until s10. Most inference nodes therefore have reader_learns_in = s10 although the protagonist reached them on day 3 -- the gap between `actions.during_scene` and `actions.narrated_in` measures it.
The one investigative action whose result is never told is a.question_maid. A game adaptation must invent it or drop it.

Two premises a solving reader never gets before s10: bg.tendon_nick (the specialist trick) and ev.milliner_identifies (an offstage visit). The motive question is therefore not fair-play solvable; the who/where/how questions mostly are.

External note (not from this text): Doyle later admitted his ignorance of racing rules -- a disguised horse could never have been allowed to run (Memories and Adventures, 1924). Recorded here only as a caution for anyone adapting it.
bg.gypsies_avoid_trouble is a period stereotype voiced by Holmes; flagged for any adaptation.
